query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the 15–45 µm feedstock with a coarser powder feedstock (e.g., approximately 45–75 µm) will improve the deposition efficiency for an FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat, thereby achieving the required coating thickness while maintaining coating integrity and keeping as‐sprayed oxidation at levels similar to the baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat deposited via thermal spray using a 15–45 µm powder feedstock that does not reach the necessary thickness.
generation.intervention: Replace the existing 15–45 µm powder with a coarser powder feedstock featuring an increased particle size range (approximately 45–75 µm) without altering other spray parameters.
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition under controlled, typical conditions for bond coat applications in thermal barrier coating systems with a standard processing atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Larger powder particles possess greater thermal mass and momentum, leading to thicker splat formation on impact and a reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio that minimizes in-flight oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced kinetic energy and thermal buffering of the larger particles improve deposition efficiency and promote the buildup of a thicker coating without increasing oxidation or degrading microstructural integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The bond coat will attain or exceed the required thickness relative to the baseline 15–45 µm feedstock while preserving a dense, well-adhered microstructure with minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.baseline: Coatings deposited using 15–45 µm feedstock under current spray parameters that yield sub-target thickness but maintain acceptable integrity and minimal oxidation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to work provided that the spray parameters and atmosphere remain optimized; if the particle size is increased beyond an optimal window, issues such as incomplete melting or reduced bonding quality may arise.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal particle size range and the scaling of deposition efficiency improvements require further empirical investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a side-by-side thermal-spray deposition experiment on identical substrates using two feedstock powders: one with the standard 15–45 µm range (baseline) and one with a coarser range (e.g., 45–75 µm). Keep all other spray parameters constant.
measurements: Coating thickness (using cross-sectional microscopy or profilometry)
Oxidation levels (using X-ray diffraction or energy-dispersive spectroscopy)
Splat morphology and interlamellar bonding quality (using scanning electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the deposit from the coarser feedstock does not show a statistically significant increase in coating thickness meeting the required target, or if it exhibits increased oxidation or degraded microstructural integrity compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, because of its appropriate particle size distribution and good flowability, the powder milled for 10 h was chosen as a feedstock to deposit a coating. Figure 8 shows the surface morphology of the APS AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating. From Figure 8a, it can be seen that the coating showed a rough morphology, which is usually observed on the surfaces of atmospheric plasma sprayed coatings []. It can be observed that at a higher magnification (Figure 8b), most of the splats were fully molten and well flattened, and the outlines of the flattened splats could be observed obviously. Some spherical and droplet-shaped particles with dimensions of less than 10 μm could also be found on the coating surface, which originated from the sputtering of the flying particles when impacting the already formed coating surface.

Nb-silicide based alloys (or Nb-silicide in situ composites) are new materials and strong candidates for structural applications in gas turbines at high temperatures where the surface temperature of the alloy should not exceed 1400 °C. Like the Ni-based superalloys that are used in the latest generation of gas turbines, the Nb-silicide based alloys will require a coating [,] but must have adequate oxidation resistance to “survive” in case of failure of the coating. Unlike the Ni-based superalloys that are not prone to pest oxidation, the Nb-silicide based alloys will also need to have good resistance to pest oxidation. Contamination of Nb-silicide based alloys by interstitial elements must be controlled. For high temperature applications, alloy developers aspire to discover alloys that can form compact protective self-healing oxide layer in which the diffusion of metal cations is inhibited (very slow). For Nb-silicide based alloys, coating system with alumina scale forming bond coat compatible with the substrate alloy is desirable []. An aim of this paper is to provide an insight into the design and selection of metallic materials for a coating system for Nb-silicide based alloys.

drafts.hypothesis: Increasing the average particle size of the feedstock from the current 15–45 μm range to a broader, larger-size distribution (for example, 45–63 μm) will result in a higher deposition yield that achieves the required coating thickness without degrading the coating integrity or increasing as‐sprayed oxidation levels.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat deposited via thermal spray using 15–45 μm feedstock, which currently fails to build up a sufficient thickness.
drafts.intervention: Switch the feedstock to a larger particle size range (e.g., 45–63 μm) while keeping other spray parameters unchanged.
drafts.conditions: Standard thermal-spray deposition parameters and subsequent service in a thermal barrier coating (TBC) system with the expected operating temperatures and environmental exposures.
drafts.structural_mediator: Larger particles, with higher momentum and thermal mass, improve impact and flattening (splat formation) upon substrate impingement, thereby increasing deposition efficiency and coating buildup.
drafts.mechanism: The increased particle size leads to greater kinetic energy upon impact, promoting improved adhesion and reduced re-spray losses. The particles’ thermal mass can also reduce the relative dwell time in the high-temperature plume, minimizing in-flight oxidation while preserving coating microstructure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The bond-coat deposition will attain or exceed the required coating thickness relative to the baseline (15–45 μm feedstock) while maintaining a high-quality, minimally oxidized microstructure.
drafts.baseline: Deposition using 15–45 μm feedstock under current spray conditions, which results in a sub-target thickness with acceptable coating integrity and minimal oxidation.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to remain effective provided that the spray parameters (gas flow, temperature, distance) remain within their optimized ranges for the thermal barrier coating system; excessive deviation may alter the melting and oxidation dynamics.

drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from a 15–45 μm powder that yields an as-sprayed coating with insufficient thickness.
drafts.intervention: Replace the existing 15–45 μm powder with a feedstock having a larger particle size distribution (approximately 45–75 μm) and adjust the spray parameters (e.g., thermal energy input) as necessary to melt the larger particles fully.
drafts.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition performed under standard operating conditions and within the service conditions typical for thermal barrier coating systems, where the bond coat must remain durable and oxidation levels minimal.
drafts.structural_mediator: The increased particle size improves deposition efficiency through enhanced momentum transfer and faster substrate impact, yielding thicker splat accumulation while maintaining a controlled oxidation environment.
drafts.mechanism: Larger particles, when adequately heated, have a higher deposition rate because their mass and momentum promote improved splat formation. Additionally, a properly adjusted thermal input minimizes in-flight oxidation, resulting in a dense, well-adhered coating that exceeds the baseline thickness.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An as-sprayed coating with a significantly increased thickness relative to the baseline (15–45 μm feedstock) while showing similar microstructural integrity and low oxidation levels.
drafts.baseline: Coatings produced using 15–45 μm powder feedstock, which do not attain the necessary coating thickness for proper bond coat performance in a thermal barrier system.
drafts.boundary: The intervention’s success depends on the ability to adjust thermal-spray parameters to fully melt the larger particles without inducing defects. If equipment or process limitations prevent proper adjustment, the benefits of larger particles may not be realized, and the approach may yield incomplete melting or degraded microstructure.

drafts.hypothesis: Using a coarser powder feedstock will enhance deposition efficiency to achieve greater coating thickness while maintaining coating integrity and minimal in‐spray oxidation.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a particle size distribution of 15–45 μm that leads to coatings thinner than required.
drafts.intervention: Replace the current powder with a feedstock having a larger (coarser) particle size distribution (for example, shifting to an average range closer to 30–70 μm) while keeping the thermal-spray parameters similar.
drafts.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition (e.g., HVOF or APS) under conditions used for bond coat application in thermal barrier coating systems, where the in-flight oxidation is minimized by proper control of process atmosphere and spray distance.
drafts.structural_mediator: Larger molten droplets have a lower surface area-to-volume ratio, which reduces excessive oxidation during flight and improves splat formation and inter-splat bonding, thereby allowing thicker coatings to build up.
drafts.mechanism: Coarser particles heat and melt adequately while presenting less relative surface area to oxygen in the spray, leading to less in-flight oxidation. Their higher mass and momentum favor more efficient layer build-up and adhesion on the substrate, which increases the overall deposit thickness.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The use of a coarser feedstock is predicted to yield a bond coat with a thickness meeting or exceeding specifications compared to the baseline 15–45 μm feedstock while preserving coating integrity and keeping as-sprayed oxidation to a minimum.
drafts.baseline: Using 15–45 μm feedstock results in coating thickness that falls short of requirements, with small amounts of in-flight oxidation already present.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under typical thermal-spray conditions; however, if the particle size exceeds an optimal window, incomplete melting or defects (e.g., splat unmelted cores) could arise. The balance between larger particle size for deposition efficiency and the necessity for complete melting must be maintained.

drafts.hypothesis: Using a coarser powder feedstock with a larger average particle size (e.g., shifting from a 15–45 μm range to a range with increased upper-bound size) will enable thicker, more efficient deposition of the FeCoNiCrAl bond coat while keeping in‐spray oxidation minimal and preserving coating integrity.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder feedstock with a particle size range of 15–45 μm, which currently yields bond coats that are thinner than required.
drafts.intervention: Replace the existing feedstock with a coarser powder feedstock (e.g., particles predominantly in the 45–75 μm range) without changing other spray parameters.
drafts.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition under inert or controlled atmosphere conditions typical for bond coat applications in thermal barrier coating systems; subsequent service under high-temperature aero-engine environments where minimal as-sprayed oxidation and coating integrity are required.
drafts.structural_mediator: The larger particles, upon in-flight melting, form thicker splats with a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio, reducing their exposure to oxidizing atmospheres. This should improve inter-splat bonding and the overall coating build-up.
drafts.mechanism: A larger particle size reduces the relative exposure of molten metal to oxygen, thereby limiting in-flight oxidation while depositing individually thicker splats. This modification is expected to yield a higher deposition efficiency that naturally produces a thicker coating without altering the intrinsic microstructure or causing detrimental oxidation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified deposition using coarser feedstock will result in a bond coat that meets or exceeds the required thickness relative to the baseline 15–45 μm feedstock deposit, while exhibiting similar microstructural homogeneity and minimal as-sprayed oxide inclusions.
drafts.baseline: Coatings produced from 15–45 μm feedstock which fall short of the targeted thickness and display typical oxidation levels associated with high surface-area particles.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is anticipated to be effective provided that thermal-spray parameters (e.g., flame/jet temperature, spray distance, and atmosphere composition) remain unchanged and optimized for minimizing oxidation. If the increased particle size adversely affects melting or adhesion due to process limitations, the improvement may not be observed.
